extracted.intended_audience: Illinois voters / campaign audience (free men of Sangamon, Illinois; political supporters and general public)
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-19th-century political campaign speech rebutting an opponent's plan and defending principles on slavery, popular sovereignty, and judicial authority, while modeling rhetorical conduct and evidentiary support for public argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fight upon principle, and upon principle alone
rubrics_metrics.description: We have to fight this battle upon principle, and upon principle alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reliance on 'external aids'—spectacle, marches, music, and fireworks are 'little trappings of the campaign.' Center argument and persuasion on principles rather than theatrical or opportunistic devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct the canvass strictly as a gentleman
rubrics_metrics.description: I set out in this campaign with the intention of conducting it strictly as a gentleman, in substance at least, if not in the outside polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain fairness and gentlemanly behavior in campaign conduct; emphasize substance over polish, avoid personal vilification, and preserve civility even while pressing strong arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant arguments upon truth and be willing to correct errors
rubrics_metrics.description: I planted myself upon the truth and the truth only... If I had made any mistake, I was willing to be corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make factual statements only when warranted; prepare to modify or correct claims when shown to be in error; this strengthens credibility and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms clearly and examine applications carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing, in order to understand it, is to get a good definition of what it is, and after that to see how it is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before debating a doctrine (e.g., 'popular sovereignty'), provide precise definitions and show how the doctrine actually operates in practice to avoid being misled by slogans or misapplications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish principle from fact in disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between the Buchanan men on the one hand, and the Douglas men and the Republicans on the other, has not been on a question of principle, but on a question of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether disagreement concerns underlying principles (values) or factual matters (evidence, procedure). Tailor responses accordingly: principles require normative argument, facts require evidentiary demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure factual claims and inferences are warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: I was very careful not to put anything in that speech as a matter of fact, or make any inferences, which did not appear to me to be true and fully warrantable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making claims or drawing inferences, ensure they are supported by available evidence; avoid speculative or unwarranted assertions that opponents can exploit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite correction and be transparent about errors
rubrics_metrics.description: I will thank any one who will inform me that he, in his speech to-day, pointed out anything I had stated respecting him as being erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly welcome factual corrections; transparency about mistakes preserves moral authority and reduces opportunities for opponents to portray you as dishonest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote opponents accurately; expose misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: He does fail to quote accurately... in order that the Judge shall be left entirely without excuse for misrepresenting me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When disputing an opponent's claims, reproduce their words accurately before criticizing them. Calling out misquotations undermines the opponent's credibility and clarifies the record for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish purpose from expectation in language
rubrics_metrics.description: Cannot the Judge perceive a distinction between a purpose and an expectation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise when describing intentions versus predictions. Avoid language that imputes motives or purposes not actually claimed; audiences judge harshly when speakers attribute false intentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative citations selectively to support positions
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall read from a letter written by Mr. Jefferson... Thus we see the power claimed for the Supreme Court by Judge Douglas, Mr. Jefferson holds, would reduce us to the despotism of an oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster arguments with respected authorities and historical precedents (e.g., Jefferson, court decisions) to strengthen claims; but use documentary reading sparingly to avoid tediousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tedious document-reading, but rely on documents when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: In public speaking it is tedious reading from documents; but I must beg to indulge the practice to a limited extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct argument and rhetorical engagement over long document readings; when documents materially advance a point or expose inconsistency, read key excerpts briefly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose opponent inconsistency regarding legal or political stances
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Douglas is for Supreme Court decisions when he likes and against them when he does not like them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight contradictions in an opponent's past and present positions (especially on judicial decisions or platforms) to undermine their reliability and show opportunism to the electorate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus criticisms on factual evidence of unfair procedure (fair emanation)
rubrics_metrics.description: He opposed [Lecompton] partly... because the members of the convention who framed it were not fairly elected by the people... the Constitution was not an emanation, in any true sense, from the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When challenging a constitution or political product, center critiques on procedural fairness and concrete irregularities (e.g., registration and voting problems) rather than abstract labels alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrative historical analogies to clarify stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: I defy any man to find any difference between the policy which originally planted slavery in these Colonies and that policy which now prevails in our new Territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ historical comparisons (e.g., planting slavery in colonies) to make abstract legal/political consequences concrete and emotionally resonant for listeners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal directly to the audience's judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Free men of Sangamon, free men of Illinois, free men everywhere, judge ye between him and me upon this issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage the audience directly as arbiters of truth and justice; invite them to weigh evidence and character, which strengthens democratic legitimacy of the speaker's claims.
